Chapter 2: Awakening to Injustice—School, Identity, and the First Steps Toward Activism.
Growing up is rarely a straight line, right? But for Black kids in America, that journey can feel like walking through an obstacle course that most people never even notice.
High school opened up a bigger world—more freedom, sure, but also a lot more eyes on you. There was this constant pressure: you had to fit in, do well, and somehow stay out of trouble, all at once. Teachers seemed to expect you to mess up, and classmates sometimes repeated the same old prejudices they picked up at home. Still, underneath all that, there was this quiet hope that things could actually change.
It was during those years that activism stopped being just something you saw on TV. The civil rights movement was everywhere—marches, sit-ins, protests flooding the news. At first, it felt like all that was happening somewhere else, to other people. But the reality of racism? That was right there, woven into daily life. Friends were hassled by the police, family members struggled to land decent jobs, and the threat of violence was always lurking in the background.
One day, a group of students just decided enough was enough. They organized a small protest at their school, demanding better resources and fair treatment. The response? The administration mostly shrugged, and a few teachers even laughed at them. But something changed that day. For the first time, it felt possible to push back, to stand up and demand respect, to picture a future that looked different.
Meanwhile, the world outside was shifting in big, sometimes frightening ways. The assassinations of major leaders sent shockwaves through the community, leaving many people scared and uncertain. But there was also this growing urgency—a new understanding that waiting for change just wasn’t an option anymore. Suddenly, conversations at home and around the neighborhood were all about politics, about what freedom really means, and about what it means to be Black in America.
Identity became a huge deal. Turn on the TV or flip through a magazine, and the images almost never matched real Black life. The so-called beauty standards, the culture, even the language—it all seemed to say, you don’t belong. Some folks tried to blend in, hoping not to stand out. Others leaned in the other direction, searching for books, music, and art that celebrated Blackness. That struggle to define yourself, to take pride in who you are, was always there, bubbling beneath the surface.
As time went on, the pull of activism only got stronger. College brought new chances—to meet people from all sorts of backgrounds, to dive into history and politics, to join groups focused on social change. Black student organizations became like a second family, offering support and a sense of purpose. Through long talks and heated debates, something became clear: the problems facing Black communities weren’t just about individuals. They were baked into the system—woven into schools, housing, and the criminal justice system itself.
Choosing to get involved wasn’t easy. There were real risks—arrest, violence, even death. But staying quiet? That just wasn’t possible. The drive to make a difference, to fight for justice, was stronger than the fear. It was a time of both hope and uncertainty, of anger and determination, of learning how to balance big dreams with the reality on the ground.
Looking back, those years were like a crucible—a test that shaped everything that came after. Values were challenged, true friendships were made, and a sense of mission started to take shape. And the big lesson? Change can happen, but it takes courage, sacrifice, and most of all, solidarity. The fight for justice is never easy—but it’s always worth it.
